title: Exercise: Tail-Recursive map with Accumulator
description: A skeleton for writing a tail-recursive map in pure Scheme using an accumulator. The accumulator builds results backwards (cons adds to front), then reverse restores order.
source: draft: opencode free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Comment explains the accumulator pattern: cons adds to the front, so the accumulator builds the result in reverse order. A reverse step at the end puts elements back in the correct order.

my-map takes a function f and a list lst. The body is a TODO for the student to implement using an accumulator. The pattern: define an inner helper with an accumulator parameter, recurse tail-recursively consing (f head) onto acc, then reverse the final accumulator.

steps.question: The recursive call to the helper will cons (f (car lst)) onto the accumulator and recurse on (cdr lst). Is that recursive call in tail position? What must happen after it returns?
steps.answer: Yes, the recursive call is in tail position. After the helper returns, the only remaining work is the reverse of the accumulator  -  but that reverse happens in the caller (the outer my-map), not after the helper returns. The helper's last action is the recursive call itself, so no stack frame is needed after it.

steps.description: The test case: (my-map (lambda (x) (* x x)) (list 1 2 3 4 5)) should produce the Scheme list (1 4 9 16 25)  -  each element squared.
Run it. (define my-map ...) binds my-map in the global environment. The lambda captures the current env.

(my-map square (list 1 2 3 4 5)): evaluates square lambda, evaluates (list 1 2 3 4 5) to a pair chain, calls my-map. The TCO evaluator loops through the list, building the accumulator, then reverses. Returns the pair chain representing (1 4 9 16 25).
